hook: One in four people sneeze when they step into bright sunlight.
twist: Aristotle blamed the sun's heat sweating the nose. Francis Bacon tested it in the 1600s by facing the sun with his eyes shut: no sneeze, so it's the eyes, not the heat. His own theory (the sun draws moisture down from the brain) was wrong too. A 2010 EEG study found sneezers' visual cortex reacts more to light, and a 2025 review says the mechanism is still unclear.
angle: The Brain is accused by Aristotle, cleared by Bacon, insulted by Bacon's theory, and caught by an EEG. Big number: 1 in 4.
why_now: Scout 2026-10-06 (YouTube Data API, query 'why do we sneeze'): 'Why Do We Sneeze in Sun' 10.0M (FactoHolic) and 'Why Bright Light Makes You Sneeze' 4.7M (Zack D. Films); median of the top 25 for the query is 1.5M. Our angle (Bacon's eyes-shut experiment) is one those Shorts skip.
